title: Most people would switch the trolley’s track but not push a stranger
body: In 1967 Philippa Foot, writing about the ethics of abortion and the doctrine of double effect, imagined a runaway tram that could be steered away from five people onto a track with one. Judith Jarvis Thomson named it ‘the trolley problem’ in 1976 and multiplied the variations. The real puzzle is not what you would do, but why nearly identical outcomes feel so morally different.

slides.heading: The switch
slides.text: A trolley will kill five people unless you pull a lever sending it onto a side track, where it will kill one. In surveys, about 90% say they would pull it.

slides.heading: About 9 in 10 people say they would pull the lever
slides.note: In surveys, about 90% choose to divert the trolley, killing one to save five.

slides.heading: The footbridge
slides.text: Now the only way to stop it is to push a large man off a bridge into its path. The arithmetic is the same, five for one, yet most people say this is wrong.

slides.heading: Means versus side effect
slides.text: One explanation is the doctrine of double effect: harm foreseen as a side effect can be permissible, but using a person as the means to an end is not.

slides.heading: Inside the brain
slides.text: Brain scans suggest ‘personal’ dilemmas like pushing engage emotion-related regions more, while flipping a switch engages areas tied to controlled reasoning.

slides.question: Which idea explains why pushing feels worse than pulling the lever?
slides.explanation: Harm foreseen as a side effect can be permissible, but using a person as the means to an end is not. Brain scans suggest ‘personal’ dilemmas engage emotion-related regions more.

slides.heading: The switch or the footbridge?

items.text: Pull a lever to send the trolley onto a side track
Push a large man off a bridge into its path
About 90% of people say they would do it
Most people say doing it would be wrong
A person is used as the means of stopping the trolley

slides.explanation: Same arithmetic, five for one, but the footbridge uses a person as a means, and most people balk.
